vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: A change from one line or vehicle to another on the same trip
The distance between two street corners in an American city
The money you pay for one journey on public transport
The part of the day when the streets and the trains are full
The journey you make between home and work every day
The train system that runs under a city
The place beside the track where you wait for the train
The painted lines where people cross the street on foot

vocab.text: Careful with two American words: a block is a distance, not a building, and the subway is under the ground. In London the same system is the Underground, and in a shopping centre a subway can be a tunnel for people on foot.

paras: Most American cities are built on a grid. The streets run in one direction and the avenues run across them, and the space between two corners is a block. That single word does the work of a whole sentence: if a local tells you the museum is four blocks up and one block to the left, you have the address, the distance and the direction at the same time. Nobody gives you the number of metres, because nobody thinks in metres.

Under the grid runs the subway. You pay one fare at the gate, you go down to the platform, and if you need a second line you make a transfer without paying again. The system is simple until rush hour, when the platform fills up and the next three trains go past full. That is when a twenty-minute commute becomes fifty. Above ground, the rule is just as short: you cross at the crosswalk, you wait for the white signal, and you never walk along a street looking at your phone.

Scenario 1
You are at the hotel and the meeting is six blocks away. Ask a local for the way on foot.
Scenario 2
You are on the platform and you are not sure this is the right line. Ask the person next to you.
Scenario 3
It is rush hour, the trains are full and you have a meeting in twenty minutes. Explain the situation and ask for another option.

practice.title: Turn each cue into a full sentence. Use the preposition in brackets.
items: The station / the corner of Fifth and Main.
on
Get / the train at the second stop.
off
Walk / the park to the museum.
across
The crosswalk / the bank and the hotel.
between

items.situation: You are outside the hotel and you need the subway station, but you cannot see it.
tips: Start with Excuse me, then ask where it is.
Ask how many blocks, not how many metres.

items.situation: You are on the platform and two lines stop there. You need the one that goes downtown.
tips: Ask about the train, not about the city.
"Does this train go to...?" is enough.

items.situation: The machine asks for the fare and you do not know how much a single ride costs.
tips: Ask about the price of one ride.
Use the word fare in the question.

items.situation: You have to change lines and you are not sure whether you pay again.
tips: The name of the change is one word.
Ask whether the transfer is free.

items.situation: A colleague asks how you get to the office every day.
tips: Describe the whole journey with prepositions of movement.
The daily journey has a name: your commute.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model answers
list: The station is on the corner of Fifth and Main.
Get off the train at the second stop.
Walk across the park to the museum.
The crosswalk is between the bank and the hotel.
answerkey.note: These are models, not the only correct answers. Any natural sentence with the right preposition works.

listenings.text: Good morning and welcome aboard. This is a downtown express train. The next stop is Union Square, where you can make a transfer to the green line at no extra cost. Please stand back from the edge of the platform while the doors are closing. During rush hour we run one train every three minutes, so do not run for this one. The fare gates at Union Square are on the upper level, next to the exit. Thank you for riding with us.

Of course, I can help you find it. Turn right when you leave the hotel and walk along this avenue for three blocks. You will pass a small park on your left. At the third corner there is a crosswalk. Cross there, and the subway entrance is on the other side, between a coffee shop and a bank. It is about eight minutes on foot, but at rush hour the sidewalk is slow, so give yourself twelve.

extra_audio.text: First, Thiago leaves the hotel and walks three blocks along the avenue. Then he crosses at the crosswalk and goes down to the subway. After that, he pays the fare and waits on the platform. Next, he makes a transfer to the green line at Union Square. Finally, he gets off two stops later and walks across the park to the office.
